https://tribuneonlineng.com/future-of-ed.text: Add as a preferred source The Deputy Vice Chancellor, Academic, University of Ibadan, Professor Juwon Arotiba, has said the future of education must go beyond the classroom and equip learners with the capacity to identify problems, design solutions, and create value. Professor Arotiba stated this in an address delivered on behalf of the Vice Chancellor, Professor Kayode Adebowale, at the opening of a TETFund-sponsored Train-the-Trainer workshop, organised by the Centre for Entrepreneurship and Innovation (CEI) of the university. The theme of the workshop was ‘Start-up Entrepreneurship and Business Planning,’ with participants including executive members of the Students’ Union, members of the students’ representative council, presidents of faculties, chairpersons of departments, hall chairpersons, and student entrepreneurs and innovators. Professor Arotiba said the theme was timely, given an era defined by rapid technological change and global interconnectivity, and in which entrepreneurship has become the cornerstone of sustainable development, and a mindset that values creativity, resilience, and innovation. He noted that by training trainers, impact is multiplied, and educators are empowered to inspire a generation of innovators capable of transforming Nigeria’s economy. He added that opportunities today are increasingly digital, noting that from precision agriculture to fintech, from health innovation to creative industries, the digital economy offers limitless possibilities. He stated that the challenge before the university is to ensure that its graduates are not merely consumers of technology but creators, capable of building enterprises that compete globally while addressing local needs. READ ALSO: AI in education: Help or hindrance? He, therefore, urged every participant to approach the workshop with curiosity and commitment, to learn, collaborate, and experiment. He added that the skills they acquire would not only strengthen their ventures but also contribute to national development. Professor Arotiba further stated that academics must continue to bridge the gap between theory and practice, between town and gown, to ensure that research and teaching translate into tangible societal progress. He reaffirmed the university’s dedication to fostering entrepreneurship as a pillar of academic excellence, and nurturing a culture where innovation is not an exception but the norm, where every idea has the potential to become an enterprise, and where education truly empowers transformation. He commended the CEI for its visionary leadership and TETFund for its unwavering support in advancing entrepreneurial education within the university. The director of the Centre for Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Professor Sherifat Aboaba, reiterated its commitment to promoting entrepreneurship education and cultivating an entrepreneurial culture within the university. She stated that the workshop was carefully designed to prepare student leaders not only to understand the principles of entrepreneurship and business planning, but also to serve as peer educators, mentors, and ambassadors of entrepreneurship within their various faculties, departments, associations, and the wider student community. To achieve the objectives of the one-day workshop, participants were engaged in interactive sessions covering the fundamentals of entrepreneurship, opportunity identification, creativity and innovation, business model development, business planning, financial literacy, marketing strategies, access to funding opportunities, and effective facilitation techniques. The sessions, designed to provide both theoretical understanding and practical tools that participants could immediately apply, were facilitated by CEO, Soupah Limited, Understanding Start-up Entrepreneurship and the Ecosystem, Ms Ifeoluwa Olatayo; Prudencia Resources Limited – Start-up Financing and Business Planning, Mr Abayomi Ogunsanya; Dean of Students, UI – Emotional Intelligence for Entrepreneurial Leadership and Start-up Success, Professor Ademola Lewis and CEI Facilitator, Seasoned Entrepreneur Educator – Nurturing the Next Generation of UI’s Innovators and Entrepreneurs Mrs Olubukola Yomi-Akinola Goodwill messages were delivered by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Research, Innovation and Strategic Partnerships, Professor Simisola Akintola; a Digital Finance Data Specialist at the Sanofi Innovation Hub, Budapest, Hungary, Dr Ibrahim Hammed and president of the UI Students’ Union Mr Temidayo Sewanu Adeboye. He said news that autonomous agents allegedly infiltrated American university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission, further proved that need. “We now know it wasn’t just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation,” Albanese said. https://thecolgatemaroonnews.com/72042/a.text: Categories: Arts & Features Ryan Family Film Series Depicts the Holocaust Through Uncommon Perspective Sam Chittick , Contributing Writer September 30, 2026 Image courtesy of Independent Picture House “The Shop On Main Street” (1965), the third installment of Colgate University’s Ryan Family Film Series this semester, delivers a powerful, uncommon narrative about the Holocaust. Directed by Ján Kadár and Elmar Klos, the film is based on Ladislav Grosman’s short story of the same name, which he adapted into the screenplay with the directors. Set in 1942 in a small Slovak town, it follows struggling, listless and good-natured carpenter Antonín “Tono” Brtko after his brother-in-law, the town’s fascist commander, appoints him the Aryan controller of a button shop. When Tono arrives at the shop, he meets its owner, Rosalia Lautmann, a mostly deaf elderly Jewish widow who seems largely oblivious to the war unfolding around her. From there, the film takes off, tugging at viewers’ heartstrings with its compelling performances and touching story while confronting Slovakia’s complicity in the Holocaust. The film shines in many ways, but perhaps its greatest strength is the performances of Ida Kamińska as Mrs. Lautmann and Jozef Kroner as Tono. Kamińska perfectly delivers the stubborn earnestness of a grandmother whose presence puts viewers at ease. As the film picks up pace and takes a more serious turn, Kamińska does not miss a beat. She delivers a heartbreaking performance that calls upon her versatility and experience from her extensive past in Yiddish theater. Kroner delivers an equally gripping portrayal of Tono, throwing viewers headfirst into the mind of a man caught between his morality and the deeply human desire for a better life. Kroner particularly shines as Tono begins to unravel, ultimately delivering a profound portrayal of a man torn apart by guilt. Yet discussing the performances separately does them a disservice. Much of the film’s impact comes from the on-screen chemistry between the phenomenal actors as their relationship grows. Kamińska received an Academy Award nomination in 1967 for best actress for the performance, becoming the first Yiddish actress to receive the nomination. While the word “experimental” is not typically associated with historical narrative, “The Shop On Main Street” earns the description. Its avant-garde cinematography combined with its ability to move between profound realism and experimental absurdity helps explain the film’s enduring, genre-bending legacy more than 60 years after its debut. These techniques also drive the plot, pushing the unusual narrative forward. The film does not attempt to portray the full scale of the Holocaust. Instead, it focuses on its two main characters, their evolving relationship and the madness that grows around them to illustrate the personal consequences of the Holocaust. Paradoxically, the film’s experimentalism grounds Tono and Mrs. Lautmann’s relationship and makes it all the more impactful. The film also confronts the guilt surrounding Slovakia’s collaboration with the Nazi’s. Tono appears to represent an ordinary Slovak caught between financial self-interest and morality, struggling to find his footing within a political system he does not fully support. By accepting authority over Mrs. Lautmann’s shop, Tono participates in the system despite not embracing its ideology. He repeatedly justifies his involvement through the money he stands to gain. In that way, his character speaks to questions of complicity and guilt without offering them as justification. The film was initially released at various film festivals where it received many accolades. It later won an Academy Award in 1966 for Best Foreign Language Film. The film’s uncommon perspective and historical significance work hand in hand with its strong lead actors and dynamic storytelling to produce a timeless work. Carrying on the legacy of historically significant films like this is important as we consider how much the world has changed and the issues we choose to speak on. Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty Images Elena Kagan Kagan says supreme court conservatives have made US political system ‘a nightmare’ Liberal justice says recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance have undermined democracy and polarized US even more US politics live – latest updates Anna Betts Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.57 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Elena Kagan criticized rulings made by the US supreme court’s conservative majority this week, arguing that its recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance had undermined America’s democracy. “The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works,” said Kagan, one of the court’s three liberal justices, during a discussion at Catholic University’s law school in Washington DC on Tuesday, according to multiple reports. She emphasized that the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, “has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should”. Kagan’s remarks come just two weeks before the midterm elections and amid battles over congressional redistricting . Earlier this year, the supreme court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map, effectively gutting a major section of the Voting Rights Act. In June, the court also struck down campaign finance restrictions limiting how much political parties may spend on candidates. Both decisions were split 6-3 along ideological lines. During Tuesday’s discussion, Kagan, who was appointed by Barack Obama, described voting rights as “foundational” and said: “If you basically get democracy down, if you get a well-functioning, healthy political system then you can count on that political system for a wide range of outcomes.” Kagan also took aim at the court’s 2019 decision that held that federal courts should not police a practice known as partisan gerrymandering. As a result, she said, “both political parties have been engaged in a race ​to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting ​equality”. Kagan said that decision was pushing political candidates “away from the center, toward the wings, toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about ⁠any more is being primaried”. “It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she continued. “In ​this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who ​vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly, for twelve weeks Sign up to How we win Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk. after newsletter promotion Kagan also criticized the court’s decisions on campaign finance rules, and the increasing amounts of money in politics. “The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare,” she said. “And they’re right.” Explore more on these topics Elena Kagan US voting rights US political financing US supreme court US politics US constitution and civil liberties news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/08/egyp.text: Egypt has announced a new natural gas discovery in the Mediterranean Sea, with initial estimates pointing to around 200 billion cubic feet in the reservoir of the exploratory well "Nasim-1X".Cairo hopes the discovery will help support domestic gas production and reduce reliance on imports.The Egyptian Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources said on Friday that drilling and appraisal work at the well, located in the Taiba concession area, had revealed a gas-bearing layer with a net thickness of around 15 metres, featuring distinct geological and petrophysical characteristics.Technical and reservoir studies are still under way to determine the volumes that can be produced, assess possible daily production rates and evaluate the commercial viability of the discovery.The ministry has not announced a date for the start of production.Pipeline planned to speed up use of the discoveryEgypt plans to connect the well to existing production facilities via a pipeline about 22 kilometres long, linking it to the Abu Madi - El Gamil pipeline. This is intended to make use of the available infrastructure and shorten the time needed to begin production.Italian company Eni is operating the Taiba concession in partnership with Australian company Woodside, while Egyptian firm Petrobel carried out the drilling work on behalf of the partners.The Ministry of Petroleum attributed the positive results to higher investment and exploration activity, noting an improved investment climate and progress in settling overdue financial receivables owed to foreign companies working in the energy sector.Egypt is seeking to increase its domestic natural gas production after a decline in output in recent years led to greater dependence on gas imports to meet market demand.Cairo is relying on the development of new discoveries and faster exploration work to strengthen local supplies, amid strong gas demand from the electricity and industrial sectors.
